description: Scale a baking recipe without a sunken cake. Flour, sugar, and butter scale in full, leavening and salt get adjusted, and the pan has to match the batch.

examples.result: The doubled cake uses 4 cups flour, 2 cups sugar, 4 eggs, 1 cup butter, and 1 1/2 teaspoons baking powder.
steps: Flour: 2 cups × 2 = 4 cups. Sugar: 1 cup × 2 = 2 cups. Butter: 1/2 cup × 2 = 1 cup.
Eggs: 2 × 2 = 4. Baking powder: 1 teaspoon × 1 1/2 = 1 1/2 teaspoons, not 2.
examples.title: A cake for 8, doubled to serve 16

examples.result: The halved loaf uses 1 1/2 cups flour, 3/4 cup water, 1/2 teaspoon yeast, and 3/4 teaspoon salt.
steps: Write down the factor: 1 loaf ÷ 2 loaves = 0.5.
Flour: 3 cups × 0.5 = 1 1/2 cups. Water: 1 1/2 cups × 0.5 = 3/4 cup.
Yeast: 1 teaspoon × 0.5 = 1/2 teaspoon. Salt: 1 1/2 teaspoons × 0.5 = 3/4 teaspoon.
examples.title: A two loaf bread recipe, halved to one loaf

faqs.answer: Use about 1 1/2 times the leavening when doubling, not double. The common rule of thumb is about three-quarters of the linear amount when scaling up. Too much baking powder or soda makes a cake rise fast, then sink, and can taste metallic.
faqs.question: How much baking powder do I use when I double a cake?

faqs.answer: Yes, and it matters more in baking than in cooking. A cup of flour can weigh anywhere from 120 g to 145 g depending on how it is scooped, and that difference triples when you triple the recipe. Weigh in grams and the scaling stays exact.
faqs.question: Should I weigh ingredients when scaling a baking recipe?

faqs.answer: Match the pan area to the factor, so the batter depth stays the same as the original. A doubled cake needs a pan about twice the area, or two pans. Batter that is twice as deep takes much longer to bake and may burn on top before the middle sets.
faqs.question: What size pan do I need for a scaled baking recipe?

faqs.answer: No. Baking time follows batter depth and pan size, not quantity. If the depth is the same, the time is about the same. If the batter is deeper, it takes longer. Check for doneness early either way.
faqs.question: Do I double the baking time when I double a recipe?

faqs.answer: Yes, but not by doubling. Use about 1 1/2 times the yeast when doubling a bread recipe, and watch the dough rather than the clock. A bigger dough ferments a little faster, so it may be ready sooner than you expect.
faqs.question: Can I double the yeast in a bread recipe?

faqs.answer: Yes. Halving is straightforward in baking: halve everything exactly, including the leavening. The only awkward part is an odd number of eggs, where you beat one egg and use half of it, about 1 1/2 tablespoons.
faqs.question: Can I halve a baking recipe?

felicityNote: Baking is chemistry with better smells. I weigh the flour, I hold back the leavening, and I never trust the clock on a scaled bake.

formula.text: Scale factor = desired servings ÷ original servings. Scaled amount = original amount × scale factor. Leavening scales to about three-quarters of the linear amount when scaling up.

howToSteps.name: Find the factor
howToSteps.text: Divide the servings you want by the servings the recipe makes. A cake for 8 made for 16 has a factor of 2.

howToSteps.name: Weigh the dry ingredients
howToSteps.text: Convert cups to grams before scaling. A cup of flour varies by how it is scooped, and that error multiplies with the batch.

howToSteps.name: Scale the bulk in full
howToSteps.text: Flour, sugar, butter, eggs, and liquids scale by the full factor. Work down the list and multiply each one.

howToSteps.name: Hold back the leavening
howToSteps.text: Baking powder, baking soda, and yeast get about three-quarters of the linear amount when scaling up. When doubling, that is about 1 1/2 times.

howToSteps.name: Match the pan and check early
howToSteps.text: Use a pan that keeps the batter depth the same as the original. Check for doneness early, because a scaled bake rarely follows the original time exactly.

title: Scale a Baking Recipe: What to Adjust
tutorial: Baking is the least forgiving kind of scaling, because a cake cannot be tasted and fixed halfway through. Once the batter is in the oven, the chemistry runs on its own. That is why baking has rules that cooking does not: the leavening gets held back, the flour gets weighed, and the pan gets matched to the batch. Get those three right and a scaled bake behaves like the original.

The bulk ingredients scale in full. Flour, sugar, butter, eggs, milk, and oil all multiply by the factor, exactly as the maths says. A cake for 8 doubled to 16 uses 4 cups of flour instead of 2, 2 cups of sugar instead of 1, and 4 eggs instead of 2. The scaler above does this one ingredient at a time, so you can work down the list and write the scaled amounts before you start.

Leavening is the exception, and it is the one that ruins scaled bakes. Baking powder, baking soda, and yeast do not scale linearly. The common rule of thumb is to use about three-quarters of the linear amount when scaling up, which means about 1 1/2 times the baking powder when doubling, not double. Too much leavening makes a cake shoot up in the oven and then sink in the middle, and it can leave a metallic or soapy taste. When scaling down, halve the leavening exactly. The adjustment only applies going up.

Weighing matters more here than anywhere else. A cup of flour can weigh anywhere from 120 g to 145 g depending on whether it is spooned or scooped, and that difference multiplies with the batch. At a factor of 3, a heavy cup turns into nearly an extra cup of flour. Convert to grams before scaling, and the numbers stay exact at any factor. A large egg is about 50 g out of the shell, which makes egg maths easy too.

The pan is the last piece. Batter depth sets the baking time, so the pan area has to match the factor. A doubled cake needs a pan about twice the area, or two pans, so the batter sits at the same depth as the original. A tripled cake in the original pan will be three times as deep and may burn on top before the middle sets. Check for doneness early on any scaled bake, and trust the toothpick, not the clock. And if the scaled bake leaves extra cake, it keeps well wrapped in the fridge for a few days, or sliced and frozen.
